title: Villers-Cotterêts to the Panthéon: the General's Son, the Serial Machine, and the Long Return
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Villers-Cotterêts, 46 rue de Lormet: the general's son is born
stops.date_confidence: attested; the day is fixed by the Société des Amis d'Alexandre Dumas chronology and by fr.wikipedia, which gives the house number as 46. The hour is contradicted and not resolved: the Société gives 5.30 a.m., Dumas's own Mes Mémoires gives 4.30 a.m. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 49.2513, 3.0838, which fell some 750 m west of the street, to the OpenStreetMap geocode of rue Alexandre-Dumas.
stops.campa: In a house on the rue de Lormet, in a small town backed on three sides by the forest of Retz, a son is born to General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas and Marie-Louise-Élisabeth Labouret. The father is the mixed-race son of a Norman marquis and an enslaved woman of Saint-Domingue, one of the largest men in the armies of the Republic, lately home from the Neapolitan prisons with his health gone. He writes to General Brune the next morning to report the boy's weight and length and to ask him to stand godfather. Brune, who has buried five godsons, refuses.
stops.quote: MY DEAR BRUNE, I am glad to tell you my wife gave birth yesterday morning to a fine boy, who weighs nine pounds and is eighteen inches long. So you will see that if he continues to increase in the outside world at the rate he has done inside, he bids fair to attain to a pretty fine stature.
stops.quote_source: General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas to General Brune, July 1802, quoted verbatim in Alexandre Dumas, My Memoirs, Book II ch. VIII, trans. E. M. Waller (Macmillan, 1907), Project Gutenberg EBook #49678
suggested_refs: The birth house on the rue de Lormet, Villers-Cotterêts, the street now renamed rue Alexandre-Dumas
sources: Société des Amis d'Alexandre Dumas, chronology, dumaspere.com/pages/vie/chronologie.html
Alexandre Dumas, My Memoirs vol. I, Project Gutenberg #49678

stops.name: Haramont, the Château des Fossés: the soldier at rest
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence, 1804-1806, per fr.wikipedia; the January date orders the segment only. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 49.283, 3.105, wrong by about 4.3 km and on the wrong side of the town, to the OpenStreetMap geocode of the Manoir des Fossés, route de la Vallée de Baudrimont, Haramont.
stops.campa: The family takes a rural house between Haramont and Longpré, and here the general spends what is left of his strength. He is forty-one and can no longer sit a horse for long. The boy of two will grow up on the stories: the man who held four muskets by their bayonets at arm's length, who lifted himself and his mount clear of the ground by gripping a beam, who answered an Austrian officer across a river with an offer to come a hundred paces nearer. The Austrians had a name for him.
stops.quote: 'Oh! so it is you, you black devil!' he said to us. Schwartz Teufel was the Austrians' nickname for the general. 'Come on a hundred paces, you scurvy knave,' said the general, 'and I shall make it two hundred.'
stops.quote_source: An eyewitness account of General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, reproduced verbatim in Alexandre Dumas, My Memoirs vol. I, trans. E. M. Waller (1907), Project Gutenberg EBook #49678
suggested_refs: The Manoir des Fossés near Haramont, the family's country house 1804-1806
sources: Alexandre Dumas, My Memoirs vol. I, Project Gutenberg #49678

stops.name: Villers-Cotterêts, the general dies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death on 26 February 1806 (dumaspere.com; en.wikipedia, Thomas-Alexandre Dumas). The withholding of the general's arrears is [R]: no source fetched this pass fixes who withheld them. The reading of this bereavement as the centre of the son's imagination is the biographer's, not a statement in Mes Mémoires. The house of death is unidentified, so the pin is the commune point rather than the rue de Lormet house, which the research pool had reused here in error.
stops.campa: The general dies at Villers-Cotterêts, his health destroyed by two years in the dungeons of Taranto and Brindisi on the way home from Egypt. He had served through Napoleon Bonaparte's Italian and Egyptian campaigns, quarrelled with him in the desert, sailed for France without leave, and come back to a state that released neither his rank nor his arrears. Sixty years on, the son will set down in his memoirs what his father had looked like as a young man in Paris, before any of it. The widow keeps a tobacco shop. The boy is three and a half.
stops.quote: Handsome in looks, although his mulatto complexion gave him a curiously foreign appearance; as graceful as a Creole, with a good figure at a time when a well-set-up figure was thought much of, and with hands and feet like a woman's; amazingly agile at all physical exercises.
stops.quote_source: Alexandre Dumas on his father, My Memoirs vol. I, trans. E. M. Waller (1907), Project Gutenberg EBook #49678
suggested_refs: The military and prison record of General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, Egypt to Taranto, 1798-1801
sources: Alexandre Dumas, My Memoirs vol. I, Project Gutenberg #49678

stops.name: Villers-Cotterêts, the school of the abbé Grégoire
stops.date_confidence: attested that he attended the abbé Grégoire's school from about 1811 and that his formal education was short and uneven (dumaspere.com; fr.wikipedia). The coordinate is approximate to the town centre: the school building was not located. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He is sent to the abbé Grégoire's school, where he learns Latin passably, mathematics badly, and calligraphy so well that it will feed him for the next ten years. There is no money for anything longer than this, and the schooling stops when he is thirteen. What the town gives him instead of a curriculum is the forest on three sides of it, a gun, and whatever repertory the travelling companies bring through the hall: Ducis, Molière, melodrama, played to farmers and clerks.
suggested_refs: The school of the abbé Grégoire at Villers-Cotterêts, the whole of Dumas's formal education

stops.name: Villers-Cotterêts, the notary Menneson's third desk
stops.date_confidence: attested for the clerkship from August 1816 with the republican notary Me Menneson, hired for his handwriting rather than his aptitude (dumaspere.com). The office address was not located; the coordinate is approximate to the town centre. The day defaults to the first of the month.
stops.campa: At fourteen he is taken on as third clerk by Maître Menneson, a republican notary who hires him for his hand and not for his law. The pay is small and the work is dull. He copies deeds, inventories and marriage contracts in a script already reckoned the best in the district, and the language he is copying out, day after day, is the language ordinary people use about money, land and inheritance when they are being careful. The same hand will get him his first job in Paris.
suggested_refs: The practice of Me Menneson, notary at Villers-Cotterêts, Dumas's first employer

stops.name: Villers-Cotterêts, the name he keeps
stops.date_confidence: the exchange is [R] as to date: it is undated in Mes Mémoires and is placed at 1819 to order the segment. The text of the reply is attested verbatim (Project Gutenberg #49678). The meeting with Adolphe Ribbing de Leuven in 1819 is attested by the dumaspere.com chronology.
stops.campa: Under the Restoration a career opens for anyone who will use a noble name, and his mother urges him to take the one he is legally entitled to: Davy de la Pailleterie, after the Norman marquis who owned his grandmother. He refuses it in one sentence, and keeps instead the surname his grandmother carried and his father chose, with his father's motto behind it, Deus dedit, Deus dabit. The same year a young Swede called Adolphe Ribbing de Leuven teaches him how a vaudeville is built and tells him the only place to build one is Paris.
stops.quote: Oh! I don't need to think, mother! I cried, I will be called Alexandre Dumas, and nothing else. I remember my father; I never knew my grandfather.
stops.quote_source: Alexandre Dumas, My Memoirs, trans. E. M. Waller (1907), Project Gutenberg EBook #49678
suggested_refs: The Davy de la Pailleterie title, refused, and the motto Deus dedit, Deus dabit
sources: Alexandre Dumas, My Memoirs, Project Gutenberg #49678

stops.name: Paris, the Palais-Royal: the handwriting that gets him in
stops.date_confidence: attested that he settled in Paris in 1823 and obtained a minor clerical post in the household offices of Louis-Philippe, duc d'Orléans, helped by his handwriting and by friends of his late father (dumaspere.com; fr.wikipedia). The exploratory trip of 1822 is attested by dumaspere.com's biographie. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January. Salary figures and the names of individual patrons were not verified this pass.
stops.campa: He had come up once already, in 1822, with almost no money and two or three letters, and had gone home determined. Now he comes to stay. Friends of his dead father pass him from door to door until somebody thinks to test the handwriting, and the handwriting gets him a copying desk in the household bureau of Louis-Philippe, duc d'Orléans, at the Palais-Royal. He takes a room, reads Shakespeare and Walter Scott at night, and learns the theatres from the cheap seats. His own Gascon will arrive in Paris twenty years later with much the same inventory.
stops.quote: Be brave for two reasons: the first is that you are a Gascon, and the second is that you are my son. Never fear quarrels, but seek adventures. ... I have nothing to give you, my son, but fifteen crowns, my horse, and the counsels you have just heard.
stops.quote_source: The Three Musketeers, ch. I, Project Gutenberg EBook #1257 (standard 1846 English translation)
suggested_refs: The household bureaux of the duc d'Orléans at the Palais-Royal, Dumas's employer 1823-1830

stops.name: Paris, 1 place Boieldieu: a son registered to unknown parents
stops.date_confidence: the date is contradicted and not resolved: dumaspere.com gives 24 July 1824, which duplicates Dumas's own birthday, and fr.wikipedia gives 27 July 1824 at 1 place Boieldieu. The better-sourced 27 July is used. The mother's full name, Catherine Laure Labay (1793-1868), the registration with père et mère inconnus, and the recognition on 17 March 1831 are from fr.wikipedia, 'Alexandre Dumas fils'.
stops.campa: Catherine Laure Labay, a dressmaker of thirty who runs a sewing atelier on the same landing, bears him a son at 1 place Boieldieu. Dumas is twenty-two, earns a clerk's wage, and has had nothing staged. Seven years will pass before he signs the recognition, and he signs it twelve days after another woman has borne him a daughter. The boy will grow up to write La Dame aux camélias and to spend a career on the subject of who is owned by whom. In the register of the second arrondissement he is entered as born of father and mother unknown.
suggested_refs: The birth register of the 2nd arrondissement, 27 July 1824, entry for the child of unknown parents at 1 place Boieldieu

stops.name: Paris, the Ambigu-Comique: La Chasse et l'Amour
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere on 22 September 1825 and for the pooled pseudonym Rousseau, Adolphe and Davy (dumaspere.com theatre bibliography). The coordinate is [R]: the Ambigu-Comique stood on the boulevard Saint-Martin and burned in 1827, and this pin is the boulevard rather than a surveyed door.
stops.campa: His first piece to reach a stage is a one-act vaudeville written with Adolphe de Leuven, who taught him the trade, and Pierre-Joseph Rousseau, who had the theatre's ear. The three sign it Rousseau, Adolphe and Davy: the noble name he refused at Villers-Cotterêts is good enough to hide behind on a playbill. It runs at the Ambigu-Comique on the boulevard Saint-Martin, and the receipts split three ways come to very little. He keeps the copying desk at the Palais-Royal for five more years.
suggested_refs: La Chasse et l'Amour, vaudeville in one act, Ambigu-Comique, 22 September 1825

segments.name: Romantic Drama and the July Days

stops.name: Paris, the Comédie-Française: Henri III et sa cour
stops.date_confidence: attested, 10 February 1829 (dumaspere.com; en.wikipedia); some bibliographies give 11 February and the conflict is not resolved. The Christine material is folded in here rather than pinned separately: the Comédie-Française accepted Christine de Suède with corrections on 20 March 1828 [R, dumaspere.com biographie] and the revised Christine opened at the Odéon on 30 March 1830 [A].
stops.campa: He is twenty-six, still a copying clerk, and the first theatre of France plays his five acts of Valois murder in prose. The house is full of the young Romantics and of the duc d'Orléans, his own employer, who has moved a dinner to be there. A year before Hernani, prose drama has taken the first stage in France, and taken it on the first night. The tragedy Christine, accepted the spring before on condition of rewriting and then not staged, will open at the Odéon in March 1830 in a different shape.
suggested_refs: Henri III et sa cour, Comédie-Française, February 1829, the first triumph of Romantic prose drama in France

stops.name: Soissons, the powder for the barricades
stops.date_confidence: the mission and the printed Rapport au général La Fayette sur l'enlèvement des poudres de Soissons (1830) are attested by the dumaspere.com chronology and by the pamphlet itself. The day, 29 July, comes from fr.wikipedia alone and is [R]. The details of what was said at the magazine rest on Dumas's own narrative and are not independently corroborated.
stops.campa: Paris is behind barricades and the insurgents are running out of powder. Dumas takes a gun and rides north to Soissons, where the magazine holds what the city needs, and talks, threatens and bluffs the commandant's household into opening it. He will write his own account of the affair and print it himself, Rapport au général La Fayette sur l'enlèvement des poudres de Soissons; no other witness leaves one, and every detail of what was said at the magazine door comes from him. The powder goes to Paris.
suggested_refs: Alexandre Dumas, Rapport au général La Fayette sur l'enlèvement des poudres de Soissons (Paris, 1830)

stops.name: Paris, the daughter born and the son recognised
stops.date_confidence: attested: the daughter Marie-Alexandrine born to the actress Belle Kreilssamner on 5 March 1831 and acknowledged (dumaspere.com); the recognition of Alexandre Dumas fils on 17 March 1831 (fr.wikipedia, 'Alexandre Dumas fils'). The pin is the generic Paris point, since neither the notary's office nor Kreilssamner's address was located this pass.
stops.campa: The actress Belle Kreilssamner bears him a daughter, Marie-Alexandrine, on the fifth of March, and he acknowledges her at once. Twelve days later he goes to a notary and recognises the boy born to Laure Labay seven years earlier, who has stood on the registers all that time as the child of nobody. He is twenty-eight, with two plays running and a reputation built out of both of them. In one fortnight he has put two children by two women under his own name, the name he had refused a title to keep. Nothing in the registers records what either mother made of the arrangement.
suggested_refs: The act of recognition of Alexandre Dumas fils, 17 March 1831

stops.name: Paris, the Porte-Saint-Martin: Antony
stops.date_confidence: attested, 3 May 1831, with Bocage and Marie Dorval in the leads (dumaspere.com; fr.wikipedia). The biographical reading of the play against Dumas's own illegitimate paternity is contemporary critical commonplace and is [R] as to Dumas's intention.
stops.campa: Bocage plays a young man with no name and no father, Marie Dorval the married woman who loves him; at the curtain he stabs her and tells her husband she had resisted him, so he killed her. The house comes apart. Antony is played in modern dress with no Valois and no history to stand behind, and every critic in Paris reads the bastard on the stage against the man who wrote him. Six weeks earlier that man had gone to a notary and given his own name to a seven-year-old boy.
suggested_refs: Antony, Théâtre de la Porte-Saint-Martin, 3 May 1831, with Bocage and Marie Dorval

stops.name: Paris, Les Vendanges de Bourgogne: the toast with the knife
stops.date_confidence: the banquet, the date of 9 May 1831 and Galois's toast are attested (en.wikipedia, 'Évariste Galois'; Institut Henri Poincaré, galois.ihp.fr). The scene is [R]: it survives in one account only, Dumas's Mes Mémoires ch. CCIV, written decades afterwards and uncorroborated by a second witness. Pin inherited byte-identically from evariste_galois.journey.json; Dumas's own memoir places the restaurant in the faubourg du Temple, some 3.5 km northeast of this point, and the discrepancy is left for the operator rather than corrected in one file only.
stops.campa: Two hundred republicans sit down to a subscription dinner for artillery officers just acquitted of conspiracy. In a ground-floor room giving on the garden the toasts go round, and a small furious young man of nineteen stands up with a glass in one hand and an open knife in the other and drinks to Louis-Philippe. Half the room hears a threat to the king's life. Dumas leaves through the window into the garden. Évariste Galois is arrested the following day and will be dead inside thirteen months; the only detailed account of the evening is the one Dumas writes decades later.
suggested_refs: Alexandre Dumas, Mes Mémoires, ch. CCIV, the sole narrative source for the banquet of 9 May 1831

stops.name: Geneva, the method invented on the road
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Swiss journey of 1832 and for Impressions de voyage: Suisse (en.wikipedia); the meeting with Chateaubriand is [R], from dumaspere.com's biographie. Geneva stands for a route through the cantons and not for a documented residence: no itinerary detail was located. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Cholera in Paris, a fever of his own and a political climate that has stopped being friendly send him out of France for the first time. He crosses into Switzerland, walks and rides the cantons, meets Chateaubriand, and comes home with a book that is not quite a travel book: observation, tavern anecdote, local legend and invention laid down at the same weight and not marked apart. He will work that way for thirty years, through Italy, the Rhine, Russia and the Caucasus. Impressions de voyage: Suisse sells.
suggested_refs: Impressions de voyage: Suisse (1834), the first of the hybrid travel books

stops.name: Florence, the year with Ida Ferrier
stops.date_confidence: attested: the marriage to Ida Ferrier, born Marguerite-Joséphine Ferrand, on 1 February 1840 (dumaspere.com; en.wikipedia), and the Florence residence 1840-1844 (fr.wikipedia). The June date orders the segment only. The Italian journey of 1835 that fed Le Speronare, Le Capitaine Aréna and Le Corricolo is attested (en.wikipedia) and is carried here rather than pinned. City-centre coordinate; no address located.
stops.campa: In February he marries the actress Ida Ferrier, born Marguerite-Joséphine Ferrand, who has been living with him for years. They cross to Italy and keep a household in Florence, where living is cheap and the creditors are in another country, and he writes Une année à Florence out of it along with much of the Italian material begun on the Naples journey of 1835. The marriage ends neither his other attachments nor, in the end, in divorce. They separate and stay married.
suggested_refs: Une année à Florence (1841), and the Italian travel books Le Speronare, Le Capitaine Aréna, Le Corricolo

stops.name: Paris, Georges: the island novel
stops.date_confidence: attested for publication in 1843 (Société des Amis d'Alexandre Dumas bibliography). Month and day unknown, defaulted to January; the pin is the generic Paris point, since Dumas never visited Mauritius and the book was written and published in France. The reading of Georges as a workshop for Monte-Cristo's revenge structure is [R], a critical commonplace and not a documented statement by Dumas.
stops.campa: Georges is set on Mauritius, and its subject is the thing his contemporaries write around. A man of colour, educated in Europe, comes home to an island where his money buys him everything except the right to be there, and raises a slave revolt that fails. Into it go the duel over an insult, the white society that will not receive him, the brother who has become a slaver. Pieces of it will turn up the following year in a novel about a man who comes back from a prison to collect. He never writes in that key again.
suggested_refs: Georges (1843), Dumas's only sustained novel of race, slavery and colonial revolt

stops.name: Paris, Le Siècle and the Journal des débats: the double year
stops.date_confidence: attested: Les Trois Mousquetaires ran in Le Siècle March to July 1844 with book publication the same year, and Le Comte de Monte-Cristo ran in the Journal des débats from 28 August 1844 to 15 January 1846, book publication 1846 (en.wikipedia on both novels; dumaspere.com). The drama criticism for Girardin's La Presse from June 1836 is attested and folded in here. The pin is the generic Paris point: neither newspaper's offices were geocoded. Auguste Maquet's exact share of the two books is an open scholarly question and is not settled here.
stops.campa: In March Le Siècle begins Les Trois Mousquetaires; in August the Journal des débats begins Le Comte de Monte-Cristo. Two of the most read novels ever written run in the same city in the same year, in daily instalments, each one cut to leave the reader hanging over the next. Auguste Maquet works the archives and drafts scenario and dialogue; Dumas writes over the top of it, at speed, and the pages go out under one name. He has been a critic on Girardin's Presse since 1836 and knows exactly what the new mass papers pay for.
stops.quote: All for one, one for all, that is our motto, is it not? ... All for one, one for all.
stops.quote_source: The Three Musketeers, ch. IX, Project Gutenberg EBook #1257 (standard 1846 English translation)
suggested_refs: Gustave Simon, Histoire d'une collaboration, archive.org/details/histoiredunecol00simo, on Dumas and Auguste Maquet

stops.name: Paris, the Fabrique de romans
stops.date_confidence: attested for the pamphlet, the defamation suit and Dumas's victory (Eugène de Mirecourt, Fabrique de romans: Maison Alexandre Dumas et compagnie, 1845; Gustave Simon, Histoire d'une collaboration, archive.org). The figure of roughly three hundred volumes is [R], a commonplace not checked against a bibliography this pass. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Eugène de Mirecourt prints a pamphlet called Fabrique de romans: Maison Alexandre Dumas et compagnie. Its charge is that Dumas does not write his books, that he keeps a workshop of hungry men who do, and it delivers the charge in the language of the plantation. Dumas sues him for defamation and wins. The pamphlet stays in circulation regardless, and so does the arithmetic underneath it, because the output is real: with Maquet and the rest he will put his name to something on the order of three hundred volumes.
suggested_refs: Eugène de Mirecourt, Fabrique de romans: Maison Alexandre Dumas et compagnie (Paris, 1845), and the defamation judgment against it
sources: Gustave Simon, Histoire d'une collaboration, archive.org/details/histoiredunecol00simo

stops.name: Paris, Joseph Balsamo: the magician made the engine
stops.date_confidence: attested that Joseph Balsamo was serialized 1846-1848 with Auguste Maquet, and that English publishers later subdivided it under titles including Cagliostro; Dumas published no book titled simply Cagliostro. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January. Generic Paris pin: no place of composition was located.
stops.campa: He begins a serial about Giuseppe Balsamo, the Palermitan who called himself Count Cagliostro, and makes him the hidden engine of the French Revolution: an Egyptian lodge, a hypnotised girl, a diamond necklace, a monarchy walked into a trap by a conjuror fifty years dead. Cagliostro's own Compendio never reached a hundredth of these readers. English publishers will cut the book up and sell the pieces under his name, until for most of Europe the fiction is simply the biography.
suggested_refs: Joseph Balsamo (1846-1848), with Auguste Maquet, later republished in English in parts under the title Cagliostro

stops.name: Paris, the Théâtre Historique opens
stops.date_confidence: attested, 20 February 1847, opening with La Reine Margot (dumaspere.com); the address, 72 boulevard du Temple, is from en.wikipedia. The coordinate is inherited byte-identically from jules_verne.journey.json, which pins the same building; the geography lens for this file gives 48.8673, 2.3648 instead, about 200 m away, and the conflict is left unresolved in favour of consistency between the two files.
stops.campa: He has built himself a theatre on the boulevard du Temple for one purpose: to stage his own novels and keep the receipts the other houses have been taking off them. It opens with La Reine Margot, adapted from his own serial, and for a season the machine runs exactly as designed, the novel feeding the stage and the stage feeding the novel back into the newspapers. Thirteen months later the revolution of 1848 empties every theatre in Paris at once.
suggested_refs: The Théâtre Historique, 72 boulevard du Temple, built by Dumas to stage his own serials

stops.name: Le Port-Marly, the Château de Monte-Cristo
stops.date_confidence: attested: the fête of 25 July 1847, the architect Hippolyte Durand, the separate Gothic writing pavilion called the Château d'If, and the figures of 50 invitations against roughly 600 guests, all from fr.wikipedia, 'Château de Monte-Cristo'. Coordinate corrected from the afterlife lens's 48.8889, 2.1103, wrong by about 600 m, to 48.8856, 2.1033, matching fr.wikipedia and OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: On a hillside above the Seine the architect Hippolyte Durand has raised him a small neo-Renaissance palace, the heads of his favourite authors carved along the facade, an English park below it, and out in the middle of a moat a separate Gothic pavilion where he means to do the actual writing. He calls the pavilion the Château d'If. Fifty invitations go out for the housewarming and some six hundred people come. The book that paid for the whole thing ends with two words in a letter.
stops.quote: Live, then, and be happy, beloved children of my heart, and never forget that until the day when God shall deign to reveal the future to man, all human wisdom is summed up in these two words, 'Wait and hope.'
stops.quote_source: The Count of Monte Cristo, the Count's closing letter, Project Gutenberg EBook #1184 (anonymous 1846 English translation); one em dash in the source is rendered here as a comma
suggested_refs: The Château de Monte-Cristo and its Château d'If writing pavilion at Le Port-Marly, today a museum of the Société des Amis d'Alexandre Dumas

segments.name: The Collapse and the Belgian Exile

stops.name: Le Port-Marly, the château sold for gold
stops.date_confidence: attested for the forced sale in March 1849 at 31,000 francs in gold (fr.wikipedia, 'Château de Monte-Cristo'); the pool's 1848-1849 range is not supported there. The widely repeated construction cost of roughly 500,000 francs was not confirmed by anything fetched this pass and is [R], which is why no ratio is asserted. The bankruptcy judgments of 20 December 1850 and 11 December 1851 are [R], from the dumaspere.com chronology. Day defaults to the first of the month.
stops.campa: Twenty months after the housewarming the creditors take the house. It goes at forced sale for thirty-one thousand francs in gold, a fraction of what it cost to build, though what it cost to build is not a figure any reachable document supplies. The theatre is failing behind it; the bankruptcy judgments follow in December 1850 and December 1851. He goes on writing at the same rate from rented rooms for another twenty-one years and never owns property again.
stops.quote: There is neither happiness nor misery in the world; there is only the comparison of one state with another, nothing more. He who has felt the deepest grief is best able to experience supreme happiness.
stops.quote_source: The Count of Monte Cristo, final chapter, Project Gutenberg EBook #1184
suggested_refs: The March 1849 forced sale of the Château de Monte-Cristo, 31,000 francs in gold

stops.name: Paris, the Théâtre Historique: Les Pailles rompues
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere on 12 June 1850 and for the sequence (en.wikipedia, 'Jules Verne'; corroborated on the authorship detail by fabula.org/revue/document12302.php). en.wikipedia has Dumas fils arranging production with the Opéra-National, the company then occupying the Théâtre Historique's house, and en.wikipedia's article on the Théâtre Historique does not mention Verne at all, so the venue rests on the Verne page alone. The brief's claim that Dumas père personally introduced Verne to Paris literary life in 1849 through the chirologist Chevalier d'Arpentigny could not be confirmed and is not published here. Pin inherited byte-identically from jules_verne.journey.json.
stops.campa: A law student from Nantes has written a one-act comedy in verse and shows it to Dumas's son, who is his own age and has become his friend. The two young men work it over together, and Dumas fils carries it to his father, whose house on the boulevard du Temple gives it a stage. It plays on the twelfth of June and is printed the same year. The student is Jules Verne, who had come to Paris on his own two years earlier to read law, at nobody's invitation, and who is twenty-two on the night his first work reaches a stage.
suggested_refs: Jules Verne, Les Pailles rompues, one act in verse, Théâtre Historique, 12 June 1850, printed the same year

stops.name: Brussels, 73 boulevard Waterloo
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move in December 1851, a fortnight after the coup of 2 December, and for the address at 73 boulevard Waterloo (dumaspere.com chronology). That Dumas opened his Brussels house to fellow political exiles is attested; that Victor Hugo lodged there specifically is [R], and only Hugo's presence in the Brussels exile circle that winter is asserted. Day defaults to the first of the month.
stops.campa: Bankrupt, and on the wrong side of the man who has just made himself master of France, he leaves for Belgium a fortnight after the coup and takes a house at 73 boulevard Waterloo. The exile is as much financial as political and he never pretends otherwise. The house fills with the proscribed. Victor Hugo is in Brussels that same winter at the start of nineteen years out of France, and the two of them are in and out of the same rooms. Dumas keeps a table, receives everybody, negotiates with his creditors at a distance, and writes.
suggested_refs: 73 boulevard Waterloo, Brussels, Dumas's house during the exile of 1851-1853

stops.name: Paris, Le Mousquetaire
stops.date_confidence: Le Mousquetaire from 12 November 1853, and the weekly Le Monte-Cristo from 27 April 1857 to 10 May 1860, are [R], from the dumaspere.com chronology. The date of the return to Paris is contradicted: the pool's chronology says 1854, fr.wikipedia says April 1853, and only 1853 is consistent with founding and editing the paper from Paris that November. 1853 is used and the conflict is not resolved. Generic Paris pin: the paper's offices were not geocoded.
stops.campa: He comes back in April and by November he has a newspaper of his own, four pages of it, most of them written by him: literature, news, memoir, quarrels, and whatever young writer he decides to print that week. Le Mousquetaire loses money in the ordinary way and lasts three years. The weekly Le Monte-Cristo follows, which he writes very nearly single-handed from 1857 to 1860. He is fifty-one years old and has been through the bankruptcy courts twice.
suggested_refs: Le Mousquetaire (1853-1857) and Le Monte-Cristo (1857-1860), Dumas's own newspapers

stops.name: Guernsey, Hauteville House
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested by dumaspere.com's biographie, which describes Dumas crossing to Guernsey to embrace son vieil ami Hugo. The year is not attested: no source fetched this pass dates it, and the pool's 1857 rests on a dossier synthesis rather than a document. Hugo had been at Hauteville House since October 1856, so any year from 1857 is possible, which is exactly why the year needs a source. Dated 1857 to order the segment, [R]. Coordinate corrected from 49.4526, -2.5354 to the OpenStreetMap geocode of 38 Hauteville, St Peter Port.
stops.campa: He crosses to Guernsey to see Victor Hugo, who has been in the tall house on the Hauteville since the autumn of 1856 and will not set foot in France while the Empire stands. Dumas has made his peace with going home; Hugo has not, and will not for eighteen more years. The friendship goes back to the Arsenal salon, when both of them were young men among Charles Nodier's books and neither had a reputation yet. What was said between them in that house is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Hauteville House, St Peter Port, Hugo's residence in exile from October 1856

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the journey east begins
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Russian journey began in June 1858 and produced De Paris à Astrakan and Le Caucase (dumaspere.com; en.wikipedia). The coordinate is the city centre; no address or landmark was identified. Day defaults to the first of the month. The characterization of his reception is [R], generalized from the travel books rather than taken from a dated source.
stops.campa: He leaves Paris in June for what he expects to be a season in Russia and stays nine months. Saint Petersburg receives him as the most famous living writer in Europe, and receives him in French, which its drawing rooms handle more easily than Russian. He is fifty-six and has never travelled east of the Rhine. From the first day he is taking notes on everything in front of him: the food, the prisons, the gardens, the price of things, and who was strangled in which palace and by whom.
suggested_refs: De Paris à Astrakan (1858-1862), the Russian travel narrative

stops.name: Moscow, the burnt city
stops.date_confidence: the Moscow leg is attested as part of the 1858 journey published as De Paris à Astrakan (en.wikipedia). The month is [R], assigned to order the segment. City-centre coordinate, no landmark identified. The account of his working method is [R], generalized from the Impressions de voyage rather than from a dated source.
stops.campa: He goes down to Moscow and writes it as a city of gardens and bell towers with a burnt heart, still visibly the town that emptied and burned in 1812. What he wants out of Russia is not landscape but stories, and he gathers them the way he gathers everything, at table, at second hand, half-checked, and sets them down at the same weight as the things he actually saw. Russian readers will spend a century arguing with the book and reading it. He has no Russian, and works entirely through hosts and interpreters, which he does not trouble to hide from the reader.
suggested_refs: De Paris à Astrakan, the Moscow chapters

stops.name: Astrakhan, the end of the river
stops.date_confidence: attested for Astrakhan as the destination that titles the book, and for the Volga route through Nizhny Novgorod and Kazan (en.wikipedia); those two cities are carried in this stop's prose rather than pinned separately, to hold the segment to five points. The month is [R]. City-centre coordinate. The recipe-collecting on this leg is [R], inferred from the contents of the Grand Dictionnaire de cuisine and not from a dated source.
stops.campa: Down the Volga by steamer, through Nizhny Novgorod and Kazan, to the delta where the river runs out into the Caspian through a hundred mouths and the sturgeon come up longer than a man. Astrakhan is the far end of the title: De Paris à Astrakan. The cookery dictionary he will die in the middle of, eleven years from now, is already being assembled on this riverboat. He eats whatever he is offered, asks how it was made, and writes the answers down.
suggested_refs: The Volga passage through Nizhny Novgorod and Kazan, carried in De Paris à Astrakan

stops.name: Baku, the ground on fire
stops.date_confidence: attested for Baku on the Caucasus leg of 1858-1859, published as Le Caucase (en.wikipedia). The month is [R]. The naphtha fields and the fire temple are [R] here: they are standard content of Le Caucase but were not verified against the text this pass. City-centre coordinate.
stops.campa: He crosses the Caspian to Baku, where the ground itself burns: naphtha fields outside the town, fire coming out of bare earth, and pilgrims keeping it. From here the journey stops being a celebrity tour and turns into the Caucasus book. There is a war on in the mountains, Shamil's murids are holding them, hostages are traded for money and for prisoners, and the Russian frontier is a chain of forts. He travels with an escort and the escort is not ceremonial.
suggested_refs: Le Caucase (1859), written out of the Baku and Caucasus legs

stops.name: Tiflis, the turn for home
stops.date_confidence: attested for Tiflis on the Caucasus leg and for departure from the region by a Black Sea port in February 1859; the port is given variously as Poti or Trebizond and the conflict is not resolved. The January date is [R], assigned to order the segment. City-centre coordinate.
stops.campa: Tiflis is the last long halt: sulphur baths, a Georgian table that runs six hours, and the manuscript of Le Caucase getting heavier by the week. In February he goes out through a Black Sea port, Poti or Trebizond according to which account is followed, and turns for France after nine months away, carrying notebooks that will make two books and a quantity of stories he will be dining out on for the rest of the decade. He is fifty-six years old. Nine months earlier he had never been east of the Rhine.
suggested_refs: The February 1859 departure from the Caucasus by Black Sea port, given variously as Poti or Trebizond

segments.name: The Thousand and the Neapolitan Years

stops.name: Marseille, the schooner Emma
stops.date_confidence: attested for the departure from Marseille on 9 May 1860 aboard the Emma with the photographer Gustave Le Gray (dumaspere.com chronology). The purchase of arms and the mobilizing of funds at Marseille are [R]: no primary source was fetched this pass, and port-level precision there is reconstruction. City coordinate.
stops.campa: Garibaldi has sailed for Sicily with a thousand men. Dumas puts to sea after him on the ninth of May, in the schooner Emma, with the photographer Gustave Le Gray aboard. He is fifty-seven and has spent his working life writing conspiracies; this one is being carried out in front of him. He brings money, and rifles bought with money. He also brings himself, a writer read in every language in Europe and willing to tell the story the way Giuseppe Garibaldi wants it told.
suggested_refs: The schooner Emma, Dumas's vessel for the Garibaldi campaign, with Gustave Le Gray aboard as photographer

stops.name: Naples, the museums and L'Indipendente
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment after Garibaldi's entry into Naples on 7 September 1860, for the founding of L'Indipendente in 1860, and for the eventual resignation under nationalist hostility (dumaspere.com biographie, which calls the directorship honorifique). The exact administrative title and the date of resignation are variably documented and are [R]. Day defaults to the first of the month. Canonical Naples pin, inherited from the interlock lens.
stops.campa: Garibaldi enters Naples on the seventh of September and the Bourbon kingdom is finished. He hands Dumas a directorship over museums and excavations, honorary in form, and Dumas takes it seriously enough to make enemies with it. The same year he founds a newspaper, L'Indipendente, for unification and against any Bourbon coming back, and edits it himself. Neapolitan opinion asks aloud what a French novelist is doing in charge of the national antiquities, and keeps asking until he resigns.
suggested_refs: L'Indipendente, Naples, founded and edited by Dumas from 1860 in support of Italian unification

stops.name: Naples, via Chiatamone: the memoirs of Garibaldi
stops.date_confidence: attested that Dumas edited and published Vita e memorie di Giuseppe Garibaldi (Milan, 1860), redacted from Garibaldi's own manuscript and conversations. The via Chiatamone residence is dated 1861-1864 by fr.wikipedia, which is why this stop is dated 1861 although the edition is 1860; the pool's 1860-1864 range contradicted its own cited source and was not used. The Anita material is [R] as inference: anita_garibaldi.journey.json cites the Dumas recension as one of two for the Gualeguay imprisonment and the Laguna dos Patos meeting. Dumas never met her. Month and day default to January.
stops.campa: He keeps a house on the via Chiatamone above the water for four years, and in it he does the editorial work that outlasts the directorship. He takes Giuseppe Garibaldi's own manuscript, and their conversations, and makes them into a book, Vita e memorie di Giuseppe Garibaldi, published at Milan. The voice in it is Garibaldi's and the shaping is his. What that book says of Anita Garibaldi, the imprisonment at Gualeguay, the meeting on the Laguna dos Patos, reaches later readers through a text Dumas had his hands in.
suggested_refs: Vita e memorie di Giuseppe Garibaldi (Milan, 1860), redacted by Dumas from Garibaldi's manuscript
anita_garibaldi.journey.json, which cites the Dumas recension for the Gualeguay and Laguna dos Patos episodes

stops.name: Pompeii, the town coming out of the ash
stops.date_confidence: attested that Dumas promoted Pompeian archaeology as Garibaldi's appointee over museums and excavations, and that he met nationalist hostility as a foreign celebrity official. The individual visits, their frequency, and coverage in L'Indipendente are [R]: no dated source was fetched. The June 1861 date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: He goes out to the buried town as often as the work allows, in his capacity as Garibaldi's appointee over museums and excavations, and pushes for the digging to continue and to be paid for. He says so in his newspaper whenever he has the column to spare. What is coming out of the ash is precisely what he has spent thirty years manufacturing, except that none of it was invented: houses with the bread still in the oven, a dog on its chain, names scratched on a wall by people who had no idea anyone would read them.
suggested_refs: The Pompeii excavations under the Garibaldian administration of museums and antiquities, 1860-1864

stops.name: Paris, boulevard Malesherbes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summer of 1864 at Enghien-les-Bains after the return from Naples, for the move to the boulevard Malesherbes that autumn, and for the well-received public lecture on Eugène Delacroix in December 1864 (fr.wikipedia; dumaspere.com). Enghien geocodes to 48.9700, 2.3068 and is carried in this stop rather than pinned. The street number on the boulevard was not located, so the coordinate is the boulevard itself. Day defaults to the first of the month.
stops.campa: He spends the summer at Enghien-les-Bains and then takes rooms on the boulevard Malesherbes. He is sixty-two, and the Naples adventure is four years behind him. The last Paris years are lecture tours, revivals, a public lecture on Eugène Delacroix in December that is well received, and copy, because the debts have never gone away and the rate has never dropped. Young actors are making their names in plays he wrote before they were born, on stages he no longer owns any part of. He files to deadline every week of the year.
suggested_refs: The December 1864 public lecture on Eugène Delacroix
sarah_bernhardt.journey.json, whose file records a revival of Dumas's Kean and the Dumas plays carried on her 1891-1893 world tour

stops.name: Paris, the photographs with Adah Isaacs Menken
stops.date_confidence: the year is corrected from the pool's 1867 to 1866: en.wikipedia, 'Adah Isaacs Menken', places the affair during her 1866 Paris run of Les Pirates de la Savane and captions the photograph Menken with Alexandre Dumas, 1866. That page names no photographer and describes no press scandal, so the widely repeated scandal framing is [R] and is not asserted here as fact. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January. Generic Paris pin.
stops.campa: Adah Isaacs Menken is playing Les Pirates de la Savane to sold-out houses, an American actress famous across two continents for being strapped to a running horse in flesh-coloured tights. She and Dumas sit for photographs together, close, she in costume, he in his sixties and enormous. The pictures are printed and passed from hand to hand, and the story that goes with them, an old man and a scandalous foreign actress, is the kind he has spent his life writing for other people. How far the pictures travelled, and how loud the outrage in the press actually was, the record does not settle.
suggested_refs: The 1866 studio photographs of Adah Isaacs Menken with Alexandre Dumas

stops.name: Roscoff, the Grand Dictionnaire de cuisine
stops.date_confidence: attested for Roscoff in 1869, the Grand Dictionnaire de cuisine and its posthumous publication (fr.wikipedia). Le Chevalier de Sainte-Hermine ran in Le Moniteur Universel from January to November 1869 and was left unfinished; Claude Schopp found it on microfilm at the Bibliothèque Nationale, then at the rue de Richelieu site, in 1990, and published the restored text in 2005 (en.wikipedia). Schopp's find is cited here rather than staged as a scene: he did that travelling, not Dumas. Coordinate corrected from the pool's placeholder 48.7167, -4 to the OpenStreetMap geocode of Roscoff. Month is [R].
stops.campa: He takes a house at Roscoff on the Breton coast, where the fish comes in at the door, and works on the last large thing: a dictionary of cookery that is also a memoir, a joke book and an argument, entries running from absinthe to zest, with the story of who fed him and where. It will not be published until after he is dead. In the same year Le Moniteur Universel is running a novel of his about the Napoleonic wars, unfinished, which will go into a microfilm drawer for a hundred and twenty years.
suggested_refs: Le Grand Dictionnaire de cuisine, written at Roscoff in 1869 and published posthumously
Le Chevalier de Sainte-Hermine, Le Moniteur Universel, January to November 1869, rediscovered by Claude Schopp at the Bibliothèque Nationale in 1990 and published by Phébus in 2005

stops.name: Puys, the villa of his son
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death at his son's villa at Puys on 5 December 1870, aged 68, and for his being brought there at the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War (fr.wikipedia; en.wikipedia; dumaspere.com). The pool's medical claim of a vascular or neurological decline never clinically fixed is unsourced and is not carried. Coordinate corrected from 49.931, 1.105 to the OpenStreetMap geocode of Puys, Neuville-lès-Dieppe, Dieppe.
stops.campa: The Prussians are over the Somme and Dieppe is waiting for them. His son has brought him to the villa at Puys above the sea, where he sits by the window and does not write. He has made and spent several fortunes and put his name to hundreds of volumes; the house he is lying in belongs to the son he did not name for seven years. The cookery dictionary is written and unpublished, the last novel is broken off in the middle of a newspaper serial, and the country is under invasion. He dies on the fifth of December, sixty-eight years old.
stops.quote: has not the count just told us that all human wisdom is summed up in two words: 'Wait and hope (Fac et spera)!'
stops.quote_source: Valentine's closing line, The Count of Monte Cristo, final chapter, Project Gutenberg EBook #1184
suggested_refs: The villa of Alexandre Dumas fils at Puys, near Dieppe, where Dumas died on 5 December 1870

stops.name: Neuville-lès-Dieppe, the wartime funeral
stops.date_confidence: the 8 December 1870 funeral date was not independently verified this pass and is [R], carried from the research pool. The cemetery is at Neuville-lès-Dieppe; the pool's Neuville-lès-Pollet fuses that name with Le Pollet, the adjacent Dieppe quarter. Coordinate corrected to the OpenStreetMap geocode of the Cimetière de Neuville, since the pool's 49.9391, 1.0881 matched neither the cemetery nor Puys but sat between them.
stops.campa: They bury him three days later in the cemetery at Neuville-lès-Dieppe, in a town waiting for an army. There is no state funeral, no procession and no Paris, because Paris is under siege. The most widely read French writer of the century goes into the ground in a Norman village in the worst month the country has had in fifty years, four days' ride from a capital nobody can enter or leave. Everybody concerned understands from the first day that the grave is temporary. His son signs the papers.
suggested_refs: The Cimetière de Neuville at Neuville-lès-Dieppe, Dumas's first grave, 1870-1872

stops.name: Villers-Cotterêts, the second grave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the reburial at Villers-Cotterêts on 15 April 1872 (fr.wikipedia). The letter of praise from Victor Hugo associated with the commemoration is [R]: it was not fetched. The coordinate is unresolved and stated as such: the research pool gives two different pins for this same grave, and Nominatim returns the Pisseleux cemetery and the Nécropole nationale, neither of which is the communal cemetery holding it. The commune point of Villers-Cotterêts is used as a fallback.
stops.campa: With the war over and the indemnity being counted, his son has the coffin brought back to the town where he was born, and buries him in the cemetery of the place he had spent his whole life leaving. The town he could not wait to get out of at seventeen takes him back sixteen months after his death, in a box; its main square will end up holding a statue of him. Victor Hugo, home at last from Guernsey and Brussels, writes for the occasion. From here the body will travel once more, a hundred and thirty years later.
suggested_refs: The communal cemetery of Villers-Cotterêts, Dumas's grave from 15 April 1872 to November 2002

stops.name: Paris, place Malesherbes: the monument by Doré
stops.date_confidence: attested: inaugurated 4 November 1883, sculptor Gustave Doré, with the d'Artagnan relief on the rear of the pedestal; René de Saint-Marceaux's monument to Dumas fils followed in 1906; the general's 1912 statue was melted down in 1942 and replaced in 2009 by Driss Sans-Arcidet's Fers (fr.wikipedia, 'Place du Général-Catroux'). The square was place Malesherbes until 1977, which is how every nineteenth-century source names it. Coordinate inherited byte-identically from joseph_bouvard.journey.json; fr.wikipedia gives 48.8828, 2.3103 instead, about 130 m away.
stops.campa: Gustave Doré casts him in bronze at the end of the boulevard where he last lived: Dumas seated with a pen, a crowd of readers of every condition on the step below him, and around the back of the pedestal d'Artagnan on guard with his sword across his knees. The square will collect two more Dumas. His son arrives in 1906 by Saint-Marceaux, and the general in 1912, whose statue the occupation melts down for its metal in 1942. That plinth stands empty for sixty-seven years.
suggested_refs: Gustave Doré's monument to Alexandre Dumas, place Malesherbes, inaugurated 4 November 1883, the pedestal and ground work attributed by compilation tradition to the engineer Joseph Bouvard

stops.name: Paris, the Panthéon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the interment on 30 November 2002, the blue velvet drape, the four mounted Republican Guards costumed as Musketeers, and Chirac's framing of the transfer as correcting a racial injustice (en.wikipedia). The decree of 26 March 2002 and the five-day ceremonial itinerary through Villers-Cotterêts, the Château de Monte-Cristo and the Senate are [R], from dumaspere.com. The motto Tous pour un, un pour tous is widely reported as lettered on the drape but is not confirmed by anything fetched this pass and is not asserted here. Pin inherited byte-identically from victor_hugo.journey.json.
stops.campa: A hundred and thirty-two years after Puys, four Republican Guards on horseback in musketeer costume walk a caisson up the rue Soufflot with his coffin on it under blue velvet. The ceremonies have taken five days: Villers-Cotterêts, the Château de Monte-Cristo, the Senate. The president speaks of an injustice being corrected and names it a racial one, the grandson of an enslaved woman of Saint-Domingue carried in at last. Inside, Victor Hugo has been waiting since 1885.
suggested_refs: The Panthéon crypt, where Dumas lies near Victor Hugo and Émile Zola
The decree of 26 March 2002 ordering the transfer, cited to legifrance.gouv.fr and not refetched this pass
